parsed.hook: Old-vine Carignan is the spine of Tessellae, and that matters more than the flashy part of the blend. In Côtes Catalanes, the dry, windy Roussillon climate pushes fruit to ripeness, but those old vines keep the wine from turning soft by bringing iron, black olive, and a tougher tannic frame. At around $15, this is the sort of southern French red that still tastes like its landscape instead of a recipe.
parsed.wine_summary:
Tessellae matters because it sits in a part of French wine that still overdelivers on price: the Pyrénées-Orientales, where Mediterranean heat, the drying Tramontane wind, and poor vineyard soils can produce deeply flavored reds without expensive appellation prestige. The blend of Syrah, Carignan Noir, Garnacha Tinta, and Monastrell is standard for the wider Roussillon toolbox, but the old-vine designation points you toward the key fact here: Carignan from old vines gives concentration, savory depth, and firmer structure than younger plantings. That is why this wine drinks darker, more herbal, and more grounded than many simple Grenache-led southern reds.

Lafage has built a reputation on making polished, high-value Roussillon wines for export, and this bottling shows the approach clearly: ripe fruit, enough extraction to feel substantial, and a blend designed to balance generosity with grip. Côtes Catalanes is a broad IGP, which gives producers flexibility with varieties and style; when used well, that freedom means a wine can be built around site and old vines rather than strict appellation formula. Here, the region’s heat gives you black fruit and alcohol weight, while the old-vine Carignan and Mourvèdre side of the blend pull it back toward dried herbs, olive tapenade, and a slightly ferrous finish.
parsed.terroir_expression: Roussillon sits between the Mediterranean and the Pyrenees, and that collision drives the glass. The climate is hot, dry, and very sunny, with the Tramontane wind reducing disease pressure and concentrating grapes through water stress; that combination is why Tessellae tastes ripe and dense rather than juicy or fresh-fruited. I do not have a validated parcel-by-parcel soil breakdown for this bottling, so I will not invent one, but across Côtes Catalanes the common thread is low-fertility ground and a dry growing season that naturally limit yield. In practical tasting terms, that means thick-skinned grapes, dark color, firm tannin, and a savory edge: blackberry and plum up front, then dried thyme, black olive, iron, and warm stone on the finish rather than sweet red fruit.
parsed.vinification_summary: The likely cellar goal here is to civilize old-vine Carignan and build texture without losing its savory character. Carignan can be hard-edged if handled too aggressively, so many modern southern French producers use partial carbonic maceration, a fermentation method where whole berries begin fermenting inside the intact grape before crushing, to soften tannins and lift fruit. I do not have a confirmed technical sheet for this exact wine, so limited producer-specific vinification detail makes the full regimen hard to assess, but the finished style suggests ripe harvesting, controlled extraction, and élevage aimed at texture more than overt oak flavor. That is why the wine reads plush enough for broad appeal while still keeping the olive-and-herb bite that makes old-vine Carignan worth drinking.
food_pairing: Lamb kofta with cumin, coriander, and yogurt — the wine’s black fruit handles the char, while its dried-herb and olive notes lock into the spice profile.
Nashville hot chicken — high alcohol and full body stand up to the heat, and the wine’s dark fruit gives relief without adding sweetness.
Duck confit with lentils — the tannin cuts through the fat, and the earthy, ferrous side of the wine works with the dish’s savory depth.
Grilled merguez sausage with roasted peppers — this is a natural Roussillon match because the wine mirrors the sausage’s smoke, fennel, and spice while staying sturdy enough for the fat.
Braised beef short rib with black olive gremolata — a restaurant-level pairing where the wine’s structure meets the gelatin-rich meat and the olive garnish echoes the wine’s own savory finish.
comparable_wines: Domaine Lafage Bastide Miraflors — why it's comparable: another value-driven Roussillon red from the same house, similarly ripe but usually a bit rounder and more immediate.
Kermit Lynch Côtes du Rhône Villages — why it's comparable: southern French dark-fruited, herb-toned red at a similar tariff, though usually less Carignan-driven and a touch less rugged.
Monastrell-based Jumilla from Juan Gil — why it's comparable: same warm-climate power and price logic, but with more plum and cocoa and less of the olive-and-herb profile Tessellae brings.
parsed.style_profile: Full-bodied dry red with firm tannins and a savory old-vine Carignan core
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink now through the near term; the 2014 and earlier vintages are in their best window for fruit plus tertiary savor. Store cool and dark, and decant for 30 minutes if opening an older bottle to let the tannin settle and the olive-herb notes come forward.
parsed.value_assessment: At $14.56, this is priced exactly where southern France can still embarrass far pricier reds. Competing bottles in the same broad bracket include Juan Gil Silver Label Monastrell and dependable Côtes du Rhône blends from Guigal or Perrin; Tessellae is worth it if you want more old-vine savor and structure, not just ripe fruit. It overperforms for the money because it tastes built from serious raw material rather than bulk-friendly softness.
parsed.market_position: This belongs on independent retail shelves, by-the-glass programs that lean Mediterranean, and neighborhood restaurant lists where a steak-frites drinker wants more flavor without moving into Napa pricing. The audience is broad but specific: value-focused drinkers, Rhône fans, and anyone curious about Roussillon beyond entry-level Grenache blends. Collectors are not the target, but smart buyers who know what old-vine Carignan can do will understand the appeal fast.
parsed.insider_take: Think of this as a better answer to cheap Châteauneuf lookalikes. What people get wrong is expecting plush Grenache comfort; the real point is the Carignan bite, which brings olive, iron, and tannin. Buy it if you like southern reds with some grit and skip it if you want soft, glossy fruit from the first sip.
